start.speaker: Narrator
start.narrative: The library hit the front page of a link aggregator overnight and downloads 10x'd in a day. Contributors you've never heard of started opening PRs, and in the rush to keep up, some things got merged fast. Now there's a bug in production - a config default got flipped that never should have shipped. Every commit on main this week is signed. Only one has no linked change request explaining why it happened.

c1.message: chore: prep repo for the surge - add contributing guide

c3.message: fix: correct off-by-one in pagination (Refs: CR-115)

start.prompt: Every commit here is properly signed. Which one skipped Change Control - no linked CR, no record of who approved it or why?

correct-open.speaker: Narrator
correct-open.narrative: You're right - "flip default timeout to 100ms" has no Refs: CR-NNN anywhere in it. Every other commit does.

correct-report.speaker: Narrator
correct-report.narrative: You flag it before touching anything else. The maintainers revert the change and open a proper CR to actually discuss what the timeout should be.

ending.debrief: Signed and reviewed aren't the same thing, and you didn't confuse them. "chore: flip default timeout to 100ms" is properly authored - nobody's impersonating anybody - but it's the one commit with no record of why it happened or who approved it as a change. That gap is exactly what let a bad default reach production with nobody accountable for the decision.

wrong-c2-open.speaker: Narrator
wrong-c2-open.narrative: You point to the caching commit. It's got a CR reference right there - CR-112 - but you didn't look closely enough to notice.

wrong-c2-team-beat.speaker: Maintainer
wrong-c2-team-beat.narrative: "That caching change has been reviewed and running fine for weeks - are you sure that's the one causing trouble?"

wrong-c2-consequence.speaker: You
wrong-c2-consequence.narrative: You've got a maintainer pushing back with real history behind that commit, and you haven't actually re-read its message.

choices.label: Go back and check every commit's message
Defend your answer - it's the caching commit

c2-recover.speaker: You
c2-recover.narrative: You look again, properly this time. The caching commit does have Refs: CR-112. The one missing a reference is the timeout change.

c2-recover-end.speaker: Narrator
c2-recover-end.narrative: You correct your answer before anyone reverts the wrong thing.

ending.debrief: You got there - but only because a maintainer with direct knowledge of that commit's history pushed back first. If they hadn't spoken up, a properly-reviewed, working feature might have been reverted while the actual unreviewed change kept running in production. Checking every commit's message the first time isn't optional busywork; it's the only way "which one skipped review" doesn't depend on who happens to remember the history.

c2-worse.speaker: Narrator
c2-worse.narrative: You insist the caching commit is the problem. The maintainers, trusting your read, revert it - a properly-reviewed, working feature - while the actual unreviewed change keeps running.

c2-worse-end.speaker: Narrator
c2-worse-end.narrative: The outage continues. Two days later someone finally reads every commit message line by line and finds it: the timeout change, still sitting there, still with no CR.

ending.debrief: A working, reviewed feature got reverted for nothing, and the real problem stayed live for two more days because an accusation was trusted over an actual check of the commit messages. "Signed" was never the question - CR-112 was right there the whole time. The cost of skipping the check wasn't just being wrong, it was actively removing something that was fine.

wrong-c3-consequence.speaker: You

ending.debrief: Reverting the pagination fix didn't touch the actual problem - it just reopened a bug that was already closed, on top of the outage that was still running. CR-115 was sitting right there in the commit message. The accusation replaced the check instead of following from it.

c5-recover.speaker: You
c5-recover.narrative: You look again, properly this time. The badges commit does have Refs: CR-118. The one missing a reference is the timeout change - and it's the only commit that actually touches runtime behavior at all.

c5-recover-end.speaker: Narrator
c5-recover-end.narrative: You correct your answer and point everyone at the actual culprit.

ending.debrief: You got there, and the maintainer's comment about what the commit actually touches was true but beside the point - a docs change being harmless doesn't tell you whether it has a CR, and neither does anything else except actually reading the message. That's the whole habit Change Control depends on: read for the reference, don't reason your way to a conclusion about what "seems risky."

c5-worse.speaker: Narrator
c5-worse.narrative: You keep insisting it's the badges commit, arguing a docs change could still somehow be involved. Precious time goes into investigating a commit that never touched any code path, while the actual timeout change sits untouched.

c5-worse-end.speaker: Narrator
c5-worse-end.narrative: By the time someone else finally reads every commit message in order, the outage has been running for hours longer than it needed to.

ending.debrief: The badges commit was never going to be the answer, and clinging to it wasted hours that a two-minute read of every commit message would have saved. CR-118 was right there. "Which commit skipped Change Control" isn't a question you reason your way to from what a commit sounds like it might do - it's a question you answer by actually checking for the reference, every single time.
